summaries.example: Imagine asking what many different things have in common. A pebble, a song, and a promise are all “something,” and each can be thought of as one thing, understood as true or false in some way, and judged good or bad in some way. Medieval thinkers asked whether ideas like being, one, true, and good describe every real thing.
summaries.summary: Medieval theories of transcendentals explain how the idea of being connects with very general notions such as one, true, and good. These notions were called transcendentals because they reach across the usual classes, or categories, of things. They were not simply a list of words. Medieval philosophers tried to explain how the notions fit together, whether they are really different or only different in thought, and how they relate to God and the world. Thomas Aquinas, Henry of Ghent and Meister Eckhart, and John Duns Scotus offered important but different models. Aquinas emphasized created being and an analogy between God and creatures. Henry and Eckhart gave God priority within the first concepts. Scotus argued that being is univocal, meaning that its basic concept is common to God and creatures, without claiming that God and creatures are the same. These discussions also connected metaphysics with the first ideas used by the mind when it learns.
key_ideas: Medieval philosophers studied very general ideas called transcendentals, especially being, one, true, and good.
These ideas can apply across many kinds of things, rather than belonging to only one category.
The transcendentals were thought to be closely related, even though they do not mean exactly the same thing.
Thinkers disagreed about how these ideas relate to God and to created things.
Their debates changed metaphysics into a broad study of being and its most basic features.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows how philosophers build a big picture from simple questions such as “What is real?” and “What do all things have in common?” It also shows that a disagreement can concern the meaning and structure of basic ideas, not just a single fact. Medieval thinkers connected questions about reality, knowledge, language, mathematics, truth, goodness, and theology.

important_terms.definition: A very general idea that is not limited to one kind of thing. Medieval thinkers used this word for notions such as being, one, true, and good.
The fact that something exists or is real. Medieval philosophers treated being as the starting point for thinking about everything.
A way of describing what something is said to be. A transcendental can be said of things in many different categories.
The study of reality at its most general level, including being and its basic features.

questions_to_think_about: Can two things be different but still both be one thing?
Is everything that exists also good in some sense?
When we understand a particular object, do we already use the idea of being?
Why might philosophers disagree about whether the same word means the same thing for God and creatures?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says, “Every triangle is a shape, every integer is a number, and every tree is a living thing.” These statements classify objects into categories. A medieval philosopher would ask whether “being” is another category alongside shapes, numbers, and living things, or whether it applies across all categories. The doctrine of transcendentals treats being as trans-categorical and asks how “one,” “true,” and “good” can be convertible with it while still adding distinct meanings.
summaries.summary:
The medieval doctrine of transcendentals is a systematic explanation of being through the most common notions, especially one, true, and good. A transcendental is not merely a term with a very wide extension. It is also a notion that is not confined to a genus, helps explain being, and is among the intellect’s primitive or first conceptions. The doctrine developed in the Latin tradition from the thirteenth century, drawing on Aristotle, Ibn Sina, Augustine, Boethius, and Dionysius. Its central problem is how the transcendentals can be convertible with being while differing conceptually. The model of subject and convertible property helped medieval authors treat metaphysics as a science of being and its properties, although they disagreed about whether these differences are only conceptual or involve formal distinctions.

The entry contrasts three models. Thomas Aquinas makes being in general the subject of metaphysics and treats God as its cause; transcendental terms are predicated analogically of God and creatures. Henry of Ghent and Meister Eckhart make God first within the transcendental concepts, while distinguishing that priority from the distinct conceptual priority of being. John Duns Scotus identifies the first adequate object of the intellect with being, understood univocally as common to finite and infinite beings. He also expands transcendentality to include disjunctive notions such as finite/infinite and act/potency, as well as pure perfections. These positions reveal a continuing tension between metaphysics as a realist science of what exists and the intellect’s capacity to conceive more broadly than real being.
key_ideas: The medieval doctrine is a systematic account of how being is explained through common notions such as one, true, and good.
Transcendentals surpass the categories logically, ontologically, and epistemologically: they cross kinds of beings, describe reality, and are among the mind’s first concepts.
Being and the other transcendentals were treated as convertible, yet philosophers debated whether their differences are merely conceptual or involve a stronger distinction.
Aquinas, Henry of Ghent with Eckhart, and Duns Scotus represent three different ways to connect transcendental being with God and creatures.
Aquinas uses analogy and restricts the subject of metaphysics to common created being; Henry and Eckhart give divine priority within the first concepts; Scotus defends the univocity of being.

The doctrine made metaphysics a common or transcendental science concerned with the first concepts and basic properties of reality, while also creating tension between real being and what the intellect can conceive.
summaries.why_it_matters: The doctrine matters because it joins ontology, logic, epistemology, and theology. It asks whether the most basic features of reality—unity, intelligibility, and goodness—are genuinely aspects of things or only ways the mind organizes them. It also shows how a theory of the first concepts can reshape an entire discipline: medieval metaphysics became a science of being as being and, in some accounts, a transcendental science. The disagreements among Aquinas, Henry, Eckhart, and Scotus remain useful for thinking about meaning, classification, the limits of knowledge, and the relation between finite and infinite reality.

important_terms.definition: A notion that is not restricted to a single genus or category and is treated as a basic determination of being, such as one, true, or good.
That which exists or is real; in medieval metaphysics, being is often the subject or starting point of inquiry.
The relationship in which a predicate is said of a subject. Transcendentals can be predicated across the categories rather than functioning as ordinary genera.
A classification of kinds of beings. Transcendentals are not confined to one category but extend across them.
A science of being as being and of the most general features of reality. Medieval discussions connected it with first concepts of the intellect.
A mode of predication in which a term has a related meaning in different cases, rather than exactly one identical meaning.
A mode of predication in which a concept has one common meaning across different subjects. Scotus applies this claim to being as said of God and creatures.
A relation in which concepts or properties apply to the same range of beings while differing in meaning or conceptual content.

questions_to_think_about: If being applies to everything, why is it not simply another category or genus?
Can concepts be convertible—applying to the same things—while remaining different in meaning?
Does analogical predication avoid making God and creatures either identical in meaning or completely unrelated?
What is gained, and what is risked, by saying that being has one common meaning for God and creatures?
Why might the first object of thought fail to be exactly the same as the subject matter of metaphysics?

summaries.example: Think about a school library. Books, computers, tables, and people belong to different kinds of things. Still, each is one item, each can be understood correctly or incorrectly, and each might be considered useful or good for some purpose. Medieval philosophers asked whether ideas like “one,” “true,” and “good” work across all such kinds instead of belonging to just one group.
summaries.summary:
Medieval theories of transcendentals study the most general ideas used to describe reality. The central notion is being, joined with notions such as one, true, and good. These ideas are called transcendentals because they are not limited to one category, such as substance, quantity, or quality. For example, many different kinds of things can each be one thing, can be understood as true or intelligible, and can be good in some relevant sense.

The doctrine grew in the Latin Middle Ages, especially from the thirteenth century, and drew on Aristotle, Ibn Sina, Augustine, Boethius, and Dionysius. It was more than noticing that these words apply widely. Philosophers tried to explain their inner order and their relation to being. They used the idea of a property: a property can belong to everything in the same range as its subject while still contributing a different concept. Yet they disagreed about whether a transcendental differs from being only in thought or through a stronger kind of distinction.

The entry compares three models. Aquinas treats being in general as the subject of metaphysics and explains the relation of God and creatures through analogy. Henry of Ghent and Eckhart give God priority within the basic transcendental concepts, while still distinguishing this from the mind’s distinct knowledge of being. Scotus says that being has one common concept for finite and infinite beings, though this does not mean they share one identical reality. He also allows additional kinds of transcendentals, including paired notions such as finite and infinite. These views changed metaphysics into a study of being, its properties, and the first concepts of the intellect.
key_ideas: The main transcendentals discussed are being, one, true, and good.
They are called transcendentals because they reach across the usual categories of things.
Medieval philosophers thought the transcendentals are closely connected, but they disagreed about how they differ from being.
They also debated whether the human mind first knows being, God, something more general than being, or another aspect of reality.
Three important models are associated with Aquinas; Henry of Ghent and Eckhart; and Duns Scotus.
These debates helped turn metaphysics into a general science of being and its basic properties.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it shows how a few basic words can organize a whole philosophy. Questions about being, unity, truth, and goodness connect the study of reality with language, knowledge, mathematics, ethics, and theology. The disagreements also teach an important lesson: philosophers may agree that a word applies widely while disagreeing about what it means, how the mind knows it, and whether it describes reality itself.

important_terms.definition: A very general notion that applies across different kinds of things instead of belonging to only one category.
The fact that something exists or is real. Medieval thinkers often treated being as the basic notion from which other general notions can be explained.
Saying something about a subject, such as saying that an object is one or true. Transcendentals can be said of things in many categories.
A major kind or class of thing. Transcendentals cross these classes rather than fitting into only one of them.
The branch of philosophy that studies being and the most general features of reality.
Using a related meaning for a word when it is applied to different things, rather than using exactly the same meaning each time.
Using one shared basic meaning for a word when it is applied to different things. Duns Scotus defended this view for being as applied to God and creatures.
Applying to the same range of things while still having different meanings or concepts.

questions_to_think_about: Why is “being” different from an ordinary category such as animal or color?
Can “one,” “true,” and “good” describe the same object in different ways?
Which view seems more convincing: God as the cause of created being, God as first within our basic concepts, or being as common to God and creatures?
Why could the idea first known by the mind be broader than the things that really exist?
How might the word “good” mean something different in metaphysics and in ethics?
